blocks.x: Patek Philippe just released a batch of new watches in concert with its Watch Art Grand Exhibition. The free, Milan-based exhibition exists to get the public excited about watchmaking broadly while drawing them into Patek’s high-end artistry. This year, Switzerland’s finest watchmaker generously gave us fresh ladies’ interpretations of the shapely Gondolo; six limited editions and two new references within its world timer, Calatrava, and Nautilus collections; and, most excitingly, a completely new perpetual calendar chronograph, the big daddy of all Patek Philippe models. If you’re a Patek nerd, then you’ll know just how obsessive collectors can be about tiny details—which is why we’ve highlighted some of the nerdiest ones below.
The ref. 5978P-010 is the first new perpetual calendar chronograph since 2011

Back in 1941, Patek released the groundbreaking ref. 1518, the world’s first serially produced perpetual-calendar chronograph. (In English: a watch that records intervals of elapsed time, plus gives you the date, day of the week, month, and—in certain cases—the phase of the moon and other information, all while mechanically accounting for leap years.) Since then, it’s released just five successor references—the 2499, the 3970, the 5020, the 5970, and the 5270. The models comprise some of the manufacuter’s most signature achievements. The 5270, which debuted in 2011, is a contemporary collector favorite, owned by celebrities such as John Mayer and considered a modern masterpiece. After 15 years, however, it was clear that the 5270 needed an update, and the new ref. 5978P-010 is the result.
The 5978P-010 combines two of Patek’s most famous movement types

Any self-respecting talk of the former category can’t help but include the ref. 1463 “Tasti Tondi,” one of the most spectacular watches ever designed. But technically, Patek has never combined a hand-wound chronograph and an instantaneously jumping perpetual calendar mechanism in one movement.

Sure, Grand Complications such as the refs. 5207/5208 have featured the latter mechanism for years. But offering a hand-wound chronograph complication within a watch whose four calendar displays adjust nearly instantaneously at midnight? That’s new for the brand.

(Good luck snagging allocations of all three, however.)
The 5978P-010’s design combines pilot’s watches and ultra-classic Calatravas

A quick survey of the 1518, 2499, 3970, 5020, and 5970 will show you a series of watches with distinctly dressy characteristics: beautifully stepped lugs; multi-scale dials; and thin hands. The 5978P-010, however, is not that sort of watch: measuring a beefy 42mm wide by 14.45mm tall, it’s thick like a modern automatic chronograph and wide like an early-2000s pilot’s watch. Meanwhile, its curvaceous lugs and concave bezel echo the profile of classic Calatravas. The handset style is a modern take on the dauphine design that, when combined with red-and-white chronograph hands, offers a much sportier impression.

blocks.x: We don’t need to waste more than one sentence of your time in describing the following reality: watches are more unisex than ever, and men of refined taste are increasingly embracing designs technically produced for women. And while a diamond-studded, quartz-powered timepiece might not be to every macho man’s taste, there’s something about the new executions of the Gondolo that will invariably speak to certain well-heeled dudes who frequent the red carpet.

There are six new cushion-shaped Gondolo Ladies First in total. Three of the new releases come with diamond-set dials and three with diamond-set everything: dials, cases, lugs, you name it. But before we get to the gem-setting, let’s focus for a moment on those case dimensions: a cushion shape measuring 31mm x 34.8mm and 8.03mm tall is, I would argue, a perfect dress-watch design, and while a hand-wound movement is lovely and all, the point here is not mechanics, but the aesthetics. One look at the haute joaillerie versions slathered in diamonds and trapeze-cut gemstone hour markers is enough to tell you that these are more than just pretty faces. Designed as dedicated ladies’ models, they’re simply cool watches, and will invariably be embraced as such by a wider audience.

The fresh ref. 5167A-014 will surely delight fans of classic luxury sports watches—after all, it’s a stainless steel Aquanaut. But this one’s special: in addition to its sunburst blue and black dial with embossed texture and red minute track, Patek printed its sapphire caseback with the phrase “Patek Philippe Milano 2026.”
The ref. 5531Gs feature maps of Milan in miniature

blocks.x: Patek’s world timers—which are powered by Louis Cottier’s signature mechanism—are some of the most famous travel watches in the entire industry. Sophisticated and beautifully designed, they represent the romantic side of travel that originated with the advent of the steamship and the early trans-oceanic Clipper aircraft. The new refs. 5531G-012 and -013 continue that tradition in bold form: their cloisonne enamel dial centers represent Milan’s city center in day and night, respectively, offering limited-edition takes on the world timer that Patek diehards are sure to lap up…even at price tags approaching $1M. (The dials are made by Anita Porchet, a world-class enameler who has become a go-to for Switzerland’s most elite brands, including Patek, Vacheron, and Piaget.)

Powering these Grand Complications is the brand’s cal. R 27 HU movement, an automatic caliber with 452 components, 45 jewels, and a power reserve of 48 hours. Beyond world time functionality, this movement also boasts another complication: two gongs offer minute-repeater functionality with local time strike, making the ref. 5531G a Grand Complication. (A discrete slider on the left-hand case flank operates the repeater.) With its hobnail pattern along the 40.2mm white-gold case, these are supremely elegant travel watches with breathtaking dials—even if Google Maps might provide a bit more resolution than their enamel depictions of Milan can offer.
